analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue government officials who violate their constitutional rights, even if the official acted in good faith.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer or other government official violates someone's constitutional rights, the Supreme Court's doctrine of qualified immunity usually shields the official from paying damages unless the victim can point to an earlier court decision making that exact violation "clearly established." This bill would amend the 1871 civil rights law (42 U.S.C. 1983) to state that neither good faith nor a lack of a clearly established right is a defense, letting victims win compensation directly from the officials who hurt them. It would apply to lawsuits already pending as well as new ones. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially those injured or whose rights are violated by police or other state and local officials — would gain a real path to damages. Today, courts routinely throw out civil rights suits because the specific right was not "clearly established" by prior case law [S2][S3]. Victim's families and civil rights plaintiffs would no longer need to find a nearly identical prior case to have a jury hear their claim [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would bar judges from dismissing a victim's civil rights lawsuit just because the constitutional right at issue was not already "clearly established" by a prior court ruling — the most common way these cases are thrown out today.

It would restore the standard written into the 1871 civil rights statute, under which government officials who violate someone's constitutional rights can be held personally liable for damages, as was the case for nearly a century.

analysis.who_pays: State and local government employees — police officers most visibly — would lose the shield that protects them from personal damages when they violate constitutional rights, even if they acted in good faith [S2]. Local governments and their insurers would bear higher settlement and judgment costs, which are ultimately passed to local taxpayers [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes every good-faith protection for officials, including reasonable ones: a police officer or other official who violated someone's rights would owe damages even if they reasonably believed their conduct was lawful, which critics say could deter people from serving in law enforcement and other public jobs.

Because it lets any pending lawsuit proceed under the new standard, it changes the rules for cases already in court, which critics of the bill's predecessor argued is retroactive and unfair to defendants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a working remedy for constitutional violations — is significant and the direct fiscal cost to the public is minimal; the main cost is increased personal liability and litigation risk for individual government employees and, transitively, higher insurance and settlement costs for local governments. The bill is simple and directly restores the statute to its original text. The strongest counterargument is that removing all good-faith protection could deter people from serving as police officers or other officials; the record provided does not address that debate, and the bill died without any committee action, so it was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee in April 2023, and the committee never held a hearing or took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 25, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, which was its only action.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor.
It gathered 44 cosponsors, all House Democrats, showing support within one party but not enough leadership momentum to move it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who violate others' constitutional rights while acting for state or local government keep the good-faith and clearly-established defenses that shield them from damages suits, and the local governments and insurers that cover them avoid added liability.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act in the House.

for.name: 44 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred to the committee on April 25, 2023; it never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda and never brought the bill to the floor; no floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the House was controlled by Republicans, who set the committee and floor agenda.

industries.industry: Government employee liability insurers and municipal insurers
industries.note: Ending qualified immunity would increase payouts on civil rights judgments and settlements against local governments and their employees, raising insurance costs that ultimately fall on local taxpayers.

industries.industry: State and local governments (police departments and other public agencies)
industries.note: Local governments and their employees would face more damages suits and greater exposure when officials violate constitutional rights, since the good-faith and clearly-established defenses would be unavailable.

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement associations
industries.note: The bill directly threatens qualified immunity, which unions defend as protection for officers facing civil suits; the bill never advanced far enough for their opposition to surface in the record.
